findings.where: First screen as a whole, desktop and phone: the hero beside the margin line
findings.fault: Pass 1 rightly turned the handwritten note into a typeset button, but nothing in Mark's hand replaced it. The first screen now has none of his handwriting. The margin line is a dark hairline, not the red double line a legal pad has. With both gone, the first view looks like a yellow lined page with an ordinary serif site on it. It does not look like the lawyer's working pad the direction promised, where advice is drafted in ballpoint and annotated by hand. The handwriting only appears much further down, in the article quote.
findings.who_objects: Mark proposed the legal pad himself because of his legal background, and will compare this direction with four others on the first screen. Without a hand note or a red margin, his own idea looks weaker than it is. The layout round also loses the one-note-per-view move it was meant to carry forward.

findings.where: The tile's own spec: the palette roles (Margin red 'margin, note'; Binding 'nav, footer'), the type-pair note on Nanum Pen Script ('one note per view'), and the motion sketch's timeline row ('The "Write to me" label writes in')
findings.fault: The tile describes a page the render no longer shows. Margin red is said to colour the margin and the note, but the margin line is not red, there is no note, and the red now colours the PDF link. Binding is said to colour the footer, but the page has no footer. The hand is promised once per view, but it is missing from the first view. The motion sketch's one element, a label written in by hand, is now a bold typeset button label, so the 'written, steady, by hand' principle animates type that no hand wrote.
findings.who_objects: The layout round (#8 round 2) and the animation round (#9) are meant to draw inside this tile. They would inherit roles and a motion principle that contradict the tile's own render. Mark, choosing a direction, would read a spec that does not match the picture.

findings.where: First screen, the italic line under the intro: 'Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience.'
findings.fault: A years-of-experience size claim gets its own line in the hero, right beside the one checkable fact (former Lead Lawyer in the World Bank's PPP Group). It reads as a boast and dilutes the stronger line next to it.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader at a development bank judges experience by kind of project and region, not by a count of years. Client value 6 asks for 'one strong line, no boasts', and the house's 'feel the CV' rule rules out size words such as '40 years of experience'.

findings.where: First screen, the headline and intro
findings.fault: The 5-second read says who Mark is and what he advises on, but not who it is for (development banks and agencies) or where he works (regions or countries). A visitor cannot tell at a glance whether he has worked for organisations like theirs, in their region.
findings.who_objects: Staff at multilateral development banks are the stated audience. Before writing, they need to be sure he has done this kind of work for bodies like theirs in their region (first-visit trust items 2 and 6).

findings.where: First screen, the portrait frame: a tilted white print held by a paperclip, top right (desktop) and below the button (phone)
findings.fault: The tilted, clipped snapshot gives the hero a scrapbook, pinned-up feel. It leans towards the craft look the direction card says to avoid, not towards a lawyer's working paper.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank reader deciding whether this is a serious advisor. The brief turned down Kelly Wallace's craft palette because it reads as an illustrator's shop, not an advisor's.

findings.where: Palette section, the swatch grid, desktop and phone
findings.fault: Each swatch's name, hex and role sit under it, and the next row's swatch starts with no gap after the role line above ('ground' runs straight into the Ballpoint swatch). By proximity, each role line seems to belong to the swatch below it as much as the one above, so the colour-to-role pairing is ambiguous.
findings.who_objects: The layout-round designer reading the palette to apply roles, who could mispair a colour with its use.
